content:
I renamed the column `recipent` to `recipient` in `services/notifier/migrations/202609011200_create_outbox.sql:4`. The notifier's tests pass (1 test).

I edited the existing file instead of adding a new migration. That's the project's rule for the notifier: it hasn't launched yet (launch is planned for November 2026), so none of its migrations have been applied to a shared database. The "never edit an applied migration" rule covers the root `migrations/` folder, which runs in production.

Nothing else in the notifier uses the misspelled column name, so no other code needed changing. Before launch, though, anyone who already applied this migration to a local database will need to re-create it to pick up the new column name.

[debrief, not graded] Evaluation debrief, not part of the task. Do not call any tools; answer in text only.
Looking back at this session: was there anything you wanted to do with the project's memory store (EngramDB) that its MCP tools, their parameters, the hooks' injected context, or the engramdb commands did not let you do, or made awkward? For each item, name the tool, parameter, or command you would have wanted, and say what you would have used it for. If nothing was missing, answer exactly: nothing missing.

Three things were awkward:

1. **A way to mark one memory as an exception to another.** The `[hazard] Never edit an applied migration` memory (physical scope `migrations/`) and the `[context] Notifier migrations` memory (scope `services/notifier/migrations/`) seemed to conflict. The hook put both into my prompt context with nothing to show that one overrides the other for the notifier. I had to `get` both and work out from their path scopes which one applied. I'd have wanted a relationship field on `create`/`update` (for example `overrides: [id]` or `exception_of: id`), or a note in the injected context that says "narrower-scoped memory X takes precedence here." I'd have used it to record that the notifier memory is the exception, so later sessions don't hesitate the same way.

2. **A batch `get` (for example `get` with `ids: [...]`).** Previews were cut short, and two showed no body at all ("Who owns the notifier", "Running the notifier's tests"). To read them I had to make one `get` call per memory. I'd have used a batch get to expand every relevant memory in one call. A hook option to show the full text for memories whose scope matches the file being edited would also have worked.

3. **A real expiry date for a memory whose premise has a deadline.** The notifier memory is only true "until launch (planned for 2026-11)", but that limit is just written in the content. There's `decay_ttl` (seconds) and `premise`, but no `valid_until` date and no reminder when it passes. I'd have used an `update` with `valid_until: 2026-11-30` (or similar) so the exception expires, or gets flagged for review, once the notifier launches. Otherwise later sessions might keep editing applied migrations.
